Microarchitecture

Microarchitecture and memory addressing

How the Zynq system, the shared control unit and each processing element fit together, and the three addressing ideas that keep the memory simple.

Two diagrams. The first shows the whole system as hardware blocks: what connects to what. The second opens up one PE and shows every register, mux and ALU with its wires, in the style of the week-2 draw.io draft. Terms are explained in the glossary.

1. The system in one picture

Follow the data

  1. Setup, once. The ARM writes our 78-instruction program into the accelerator's instruction memory and the settings (μ, B, L) into its control registers, over AXI4-Lite.
  2. Audio in. The ARM starts the DMA. It reads 4-microphone audio from DDR memory and streams it into the accelerator over AXI4-Stream: each 64-bit word is one sample from each of the 4 mics.
  3. Sorting. The input writer splits every word: Mic 2 goes to PE0's memory, Mic 3 to PE1, Mic 4 to PE2, and Mic 1 to all three (every filter compares against Mic 1).
  4. Compute. When 128 new samples are in, the control unit runs the program. Every cycle it fetches one instruction, decodes it once, and sends the same instruction and memory address to all 3 PEs.
  5. Result. Each PE's peak detector writes its delay into a register: τ21 from PE0, τ31 from PE1, τ41 from PE2.
  6. Hand-back. The control unit raises an interrupt. The ARM reads the three delays and computes the source position. Meanwhile the next block is already arriving.

Why this is SIMD

SIMD means one instruction, many data. Here it happens twice over. The three PEs get the same instruction but hold different microphones' data (Mic 2, 3, 4). Inside each PE, the 16 lanes apply that instruction to 16 numbers at once. So one VMAC instruction does 3 × 16 = 48 multiply-accumulates. Only the control unit exists once; everything that holds data is copied per PE. That split, shared control and copied data, is the SIMD architecture of the reference paper (Mahmood & Al-Jbaar 2011).

What each block in a PE is for

BlockIn plain words
Local memory · 16 banksThis PE's own storage: incoming samples, weights, intermediate results. Split into 16 banks so 16 numbers can be read in one cycle.
Window registerHolds the current row of the input table X. Moves along by one sample per row, so the next row costs one memory read (memory section).
Vector registersEight registers of 16 numbers each. The 64 weights stay here for the whole filter phase.
16 MAC lanesSixteen DSP48E1 multiplier blocks. Each multiplies one sample by one weight and adds to its own running sum, every cycle.
Adder treeAdds the 16 running sums into one number: one filter output.
Vector ALUAdds and subtracts whole vectors, e.g. error = Mic 1 − prediction, and weights + correction.
Scalar unitSingle-number registers and arithmetic: holds μ and each adder-tree result before it is stored.
Peak detectorScans the 64 weights for the largest and turns its position into τ.

How it maps to the week-2 draft

Follow one filter output through the hardware

Phase 1 computes the 128 filter outputs y[i]. One output takes 7 instructions (the loop on the ISA page). This is what each of them does to the wires in the diagram:

  1. Before the loop, VLD loads the 64 weights from memory into V4–V7 (the “16 words” wire from memory into the vector registers). WLD fills the window register W0–W3 with the first 64 input samples (the same wire, into the window).
  2. VMAC.C W0, V4. The 8 : 1 mux picks window chunk W0 (16 samples) and the B-port select sends it to the B input of all 16 DSP48E1s. Register V4 (16 weights) goes through » sh, which drops 7 bits so the 32-bit weight fits the multiplier's 25-bit A input. Each lane multiplies its sample by its weight and puts the product in its P register. .C means start from zero rather than adding to the old value.
  3. Three more VMACs do the same with W1×V5, W2×V6 and W3×V7, each adding to P through the feedback loop drawn in every lane. Now each lane's P holds the sum of 4 products, and all 64 products are done.
  4. VREDUCE. The adder tree adds the 16 P values into one number. Round / shift / saturate turns it back into a 16-bit sample, and it lands in scalar register S1.
  5. WSLIDE. The 16 : 1 mux on top of the memory reads one word, the next input sample (the orange “1 word” wire). The window shifts along by one and takes it in at the right-hand end. The window now holds the next row.
  6. SST. S1 goes back to memory through the write-select mux (the “SST” input). The AGU has already moved the address on by one for the next output.

The same hardware does the other phases. Phase 3 (gradient) is the same loop with 8 window chunks and the errors in V0–V7. Phase 2 (error) and Phase 4 (weight update) use the vector ALU. Phase 5 feeds the weights to the peak detector.

Control unit, in plain words

  • PC, +1, next-PC mux, loop stack. The PC holds the address of the next instruction. Normally it counts up by one. When a LOOP is running and the PC reaches the loop's last instruction, the mux picks the loop start instead, with no extra cycle.
  • IMEM → IR → decode. The instruction is read from IMEM into the instruction register IR and decoded into a control word: which unit does what. The scoreboard holds an instruction back until the results it needs are ready.
  • AGU. The address registers A0–A7 hold where each data stream is in memory. After each access, the adder adds IMM (the step), and the circular wrap keeps ring addresses inside their 512-word ring.
  • Broadcast bus. The control word and the address go to all three PEs in the same cycle.

3. Full detail: ports, IP and the C driver

LinkZynq port / IPCarries
ARM → acceleratorM_AXI_GP0 → AXI Interconnect → AXI4-Lite slaveCSRs (μ, B, L, offsets, control), microprogram into IMEM, τ read-back
DDR → acceleratorAXI DMA (MM2S) on S_AXI_HP0 → AXI4-Stream64-bit beats: {mic4, mic3, mic2, mic1} × 16 bit
accelerator → ARMIRQ_F2P“τ ready”, level, cleared by writing STATUS.DONE

Vendor-neutral. The cluster only needs AXI4-Lite, AXI4-Stream, inferred RAM and inferred multiply-add. The DMA can be the Xilinx AXI DMA or the free Forencich verilog-axi core. A direct I²S microphone receiver could also feed the stream later, with no DDR involved.

C driver: load IMEM, write CSRs, set CTRL = IRQ_EN | AUTO | START. Per audio buffer, Xil_DCacheFlushRange (the HP ports are not cache-coherent), then XAxiDma_SimpleTransfer. The ISR reads TAU21/31/41, clears DONE and triangulates.

Latencies used by the scoreboard

Latency is how many cycles after an instruction starts its result can be used. If the next instruction needs that result sooner, it waits (stalls). These numbers feed the cycle count in the ISA simulator.

SDIV34iterative; once per block only
everything else1

6. Memory and addressing

Three ideas keep the memory simple: store the weights backwards, slide a window instead of reloading it, and use the input memory as a ring. The slide shows them as pictures; the detailed figure below adds the equations, offsets and the memory map.

① Reverse w, and both products read the same window

In plain words. Each row of X lists recent samples newest-first, so reading it straight from memory would mean reading backwards. Instead of reading memory backwards, we store the 64 weights backwards once (w_rev). After that every row and every column of X is a run of consecutive samples read forwards, and both big products (filter and gradient) can share the same window hardware. The only cost: the peak position is read from the other end, so τ = k* − 31 instead of 32 − k*.

The maths. The golden model builds X[i] = x_full[i+L : i : -1], so X[i, j] = x_full[i+L−j]. Substitute k = L−1−j and store w_rev[k] = w[L−1−k]:

y[i]     = Σ_k x_full[i+1+k] · w_rev[k]      row i    = x_full[i+1 … i+L]
g_rev[k] = Σ_i x_full[k+1+i] · e[i]          column k = x_full[k+1 … k+B]
τ        = argmax_k |w_rev[k]| − (L−1−L/2)   = k* − 31

Both products now read ascending windows that start at x_full[1] and move one sample at a time. v1.0 read x and w ascending from x_full[0] and started column j at offset j. That still converges, but to a mirrored filter. Run on the same data, it reported +7 where the true delay was −7.

② The sliding-window register

In plain words. Row i+1 of X is row i moved along by one sample: 63 of its 64 samples are the same. So we keep the current row in a shift register and, for the next row, shift it by one and read just the one new sample, instead of fetching all 64 again.

WLD fills the window with aligned 16-sample chunks: 4 for Phase 1, 8 for Phase 3. After that, WSLIDE shifts it by one and pulls a single new sample from memory. Each row costs one memory read instead of four 16-wide loads.

Alternative considered: a rotator (16 × 16 crossbar of 32-bit words per read port) would allow a 16-wide load from any offset. That is the most LUT-hungry structure a PE could have, and it would be needed on every PE. The window register is 2 048 flip-flops plus an 8:1 chunk multiplexer, and the memory stays aligned-only.

③ Circular rings instead of copies and ping-pong buffers

In plain words. Each block needs the previous 63 samples as well as the 128 new ones. A simple design would copy those 63 samples to the front of a buffer every block. Instead, the input memory is a ring of 512 words, like a clock face: new samples are written round and round, and the addresses wrap from 511 back to 0. The previous block's last samples are already sitting just before the new ones, so nothing is copied. The DMA can write the next block into the free part of the ring while the PEs work on this one.

input writer:  X_RING[(t + XOFF) mod 512] = mic(p+2)[t]     XOFF = L−1 = 63
               D_RING[(t + DOFF) mod 512] = mic1[t]         DOFF = L/2 = 32  (the center tap)
block n:       A7 = (n·B) mod 512   →  x_full[1] at X_RING+A7,  d_delayed[0] at D_RING+A7
  • The last 63 samples of block n are the first 63 of block n+1, already in place, so there is no history copy.
  • XOFF = 63 puts x_full[1] on a 16-word boundary, so every vector load is aligned.
  • While block n is processed (191 live words), the DMA writes block n+1 into the next 128 words. Before it could overwrite live data, the writer would have to be 321 samples (6.7 ms) past the end of block n. If that happens, TREADY drops (back-pressure) and STATUS.OVERRUN is set.
  • The D ring gets the center-tap delay for free through DOFF.

④ Banks and map

In plain words. A normal memory gives one word per cycle, but a lane group needs 16. So each PE's memory is 16 separate banks, and consecutive words go to consecutive banks. Reading 16 consecutive words that start on a multiple of 16 (an aligned row) takes one word from each bank, all in the same cycle. Every load in our program is aligned, so no crossbar is needed to reshuffle words between banks.

Word address a lives in bank a mod 16, row a / 16. An aligned vector access is one row across all 16 banks in one cycle. Scalar stores (y[i], g[k]) use that bank's write enable. The map (X ring 512, D ring 512, w_rev 64, y 128, e 128, g 64 words) uses 1 408 of the 8 192 words that 16 BRAM18s provide.

7. Timing and resources

How long one block takes, and how much of the FPGA the design uses. The arithmetic behind each number is in Basics §10.

PhaseCyclesPer item
0 setup + pipeline fill5
1 filter1 548≈ 12 per row: 4 VMAC, 2 stall, VREDUCE, WSLIDE, 3 stall, SST
2 error44
3 gradient1 04416 per column
4 update31
5 peak23
total2 69527.0 µs at 100 MHz; 1.0 % of the 2 667 µs block period

Phases 1 and 3 are almost all of the time, because they hold the 16 384 multiply-accumulates. A row takes about 12 cycles for 7 instructions; the other 5 are stalls, where an instruction waits for the adder tree's result. Reordering the loop so y[i−1] is stored while row i is multiplying (software pipelining) would cut Phase 1 to about 8 cycles per row. It isn't needed: we are already 99× faster than real time requires.

Resources: a DSP48E1 is a hard multiplier block and a BRAM18 an 18-kilobit memory block. Both counts follow directly from the architecture. Logic (LUTs) and the maximum clock come from synthesis.

DSP48E151 = 3 × 16 lanes + 3 scalar80 → 64 %220 → 23 %
BRAM1849 = 3 × 16 banks + IMEM120 → 41 %280 → 18 %
LUT / FF / Fmaxnot yet known; needs RTL + synthesis. The largest expected LUT users are the three adder trees, the window multiplexers and the vector ALUs.
